conventional_description: In conventional medicine, cor pulmonale is a form of right-sided heart failure caused by high blood pressure in the lungs, usually from long-term lung conditions like COPD or interstitial lung disease. As the right side of the heart struggles to pump against this resistance, it enlarges and weakens. Common symptoms include breathlessness, fatigue, swollen legs, and chest discomfort. Diagnosis typically involves echocardiography, chest imaging, and lung function tests.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on reducing the workload on the right heart. This includes supplemental oxygen to lower lung artery pressure, diuretics to manage fluid retention, and sometimes medications to dilate lung blood vessels. Managing the underlying lung disease - such as with bronchodilators and corticosteroids for COPD - is central. In advanced cases, lung or heart-lung transplant may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, cor pulmonale is understood as a deep and layered condition that begins with the Lungs and eventually involves the Heart, Spleen, and Kidneys. The Lungs govern the movement of Qi and the rhythm of breathing, so any long-standing lung disease - whether from smoking, chronic infection, or constitutional weakness - slowly drains the Lung Qi. When Lung Qi is weak, it cannot properly descend and distribute Qi, and the Heart, which relies on this flow, begins to suffer.
As the condition progresses, the Kidneys become involved. The Kidneys are responsible for 'grasping' the Qi and pulling it deep into the body, so when they fail, every breath becomes shallow and difficult. At the same time, the Spleen and Kidney Yang energies - the body's warming, transformative forces - weaken, leading to fluid buildup, cold intolerance, and swelling. Blood stasis develops because Qi is the force that moves blood; when Qi is deficient, blood stagnates, especially in the chest.
This is why TCM does not treat all cor pulmonale patients the same way. A person with predominantly Lung Qi Deficiency will need to strengthen the Lungs, while someone with Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency needs to warm and drain fluids. An acute exacerbation with thick yellow phlegm signals Phlegm-Heat, requiring a clearing approach. The art of TCM is identifying which pattern is active and treating it accordingly.
classical_quote: 「心水者，其身重而少气，不得卧，烦而躁。」
classical_translation: "When the heart water is diseased, the person has a heavy sensation in the body and shortness of breath, cannot lie flat, and is vexed and restless. This ancient description closely matches the dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and fluid retention seen in cor pulmonale."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the quality of your breathlessness and the nature of any cough or sputum. These clues immediately point toward either a chronic deficiency pattern or an acute flare-up. The timing - whether symptoms are worse with exertion, at rest, or during certain seasons - also helps separate an underlying weakness from a sudden obstruction.
Lung Qi Deficiency is often the earliest, simplest picture. The person feels mildly short of breath, tires easily, and catches colds frequently. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is weak, especially in the Lung position. Because there is no significant phlegm or fluid retention yet, this pattern is distinguished by its lack of heat signs and relatively mild presentation.
Kidneys failing to receive Qi moves the problem deeper. Here, the hallmark is a clear difficulty inhaling - it feels as though you cannot pull air in, especially on exertion. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep and weak at the Kidney positions. Unlike the previous pattern, this breathlessness is more profound and is not accompanied by copious phlegm or edema.
Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation is very common as the condition persists. The practitioner looks for signs of poor circulation alongside fatigue: bluish lips, a dusky complexion, and a fixed, oppressive chest tightness. The tongue may appear dark or show purple spots, and the pulse feels thready and choppy. These stasis signs differentiate it from pure Qi deficiency.
Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency introduces fluid retention and cold. The legs swell, the body feels heavy, and there is marked fatigue with poor appetite and loose stools. The tongue is pale, swollen, and coated with a white, slippery fur; the pulse is deep, slow, and weak. The digestive complaints and cold limbs set this apart from patterns that mainly affect the lungs.
Lung and Kidney Yang Deficiency also causes edema but emphasizes respiratory distress with thin, watery sputum. The person feels cold and worsens in chilly weather. The tongue is pale and wet, the pulse deep and thready. This contrasts with the next pattern because the sputum is clear and watery, never yellow or sticky.
Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs signals an acute exacerbation. Suddenly, the cough produces thick, yellow, sticky phlegm that is hard to expel. Breathing becomes rapid, and the chest feels hot and oppressed. The tongue turns red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. These heat signs - feverishness, thirst, and the color of the sputum - make this pattern unmistakable.

patterns.symptoms: ["Deep, persistent fatigue and weakness", "Shortness of breath that worsens with even slight exertion", "Fixed, stabbing or pressing chest pain that does not move", "Dusky, purplish lips or a greyish facial complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion or rushing, Cold, damp weather, Raw, cold, or heavy greasy foods, Prolonged worry or sadness
patterns.better_with: Rest, especially sitting upright, Gentle, unhurried movement, Warm, cooked meals and warm drinks, Keeping the chest and back warm
patterns.why_this_happens: Long-standing lung disease weakens the Lung Qi, and because Qi is the force that moves blood, a lack of Qi gradually slows the circulation. Over time, this sluggish flow turns into blood stasis, especially in the chest, where the heart and lungs work hardest. The result is a mix of exhaustion and breathlessness from the Qi deficiency, plus a fixed, heavy chest pressure and bluish lips or fingertips from the stuck blood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body with a dark or purplish tinge, possible stasis spots, teeth marks, and thin white coat. Pulse: deep, fine, weak, and choppy (涩, sè) - like a hesitant, rough flow.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi is the body's engine for moving blood; when it is already weak, any extra drain-like overexertion, cold, or emotional strain-further saps it, allowing stasis to deepen and pain to worsen. Rest and warmth conserve Qi, while gentle movement prevents stagnation without exhausting the reserves. Warm, cooked foods are easier to transform into usable Qi and blood, supporting the heart and lungs.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked, easy-to-digest foods like soups, stews, and congees. Small amounts of Qi-building ingredients such as astragalus root (huáng qí) in broth, dates, and a little ginger can help. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks, which further weaken the digestive fire. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi keeps Qi flowing without exhausting it; stop before you feel breathless. Keep the chest and upper back warm, especially in cool weather.

patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic lung disease gradually exhausts the body's warming Yang energy, hitting the Spleen and Kidneys hardest. When these two organs lose their warmth, they can no longer transform and transport fluids properly, so water builds up in the body. That water spills into the chest, making breathing even harder, while the lack of Yang heat leaves the whole body feeling cold, heavy, and drained.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen and puffy with teeth marks, white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak and slow; both rear (Kidney) positions and the right middle (Spleen) position are especially feeble.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the enemies of Yang energy; they smother the internal warmth that the Spleen and Kidneys need to function. Raw and cold foods directly chill the digestive fire, while overexertion drains the little Yang that remains. Rest and external warmth conserve and gently stoke that fire, allowing the body to gradually transform and eliminate the excess fluid that congests the lungs and tissues.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee with ginger, stews, and soups. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that chill and burden the Spleen. Keep your lower back and feet warm, and rest when tired. Gentle movement like slow walking can help move fluids, but never push to the point of exhaustion.

patterns.why_this_happens: In cor pulmonale, the chronic lung disease eventually exhausts the body's deepest reserves. The Lungs govern breathing and the Kidneys grasp the Qi, pulling air deep into the body. When the Yang of both organs becomes weak, the Lungs cannot descend Qi and the Kidneys cannot receive it, so every breath feels shallow and incomplete. The Yang deficiency also fails to warm the body or transform fluids, leading to cold limbs and a buildup of thin, watery phlegm that further blocks the airways. Over time, this profound weakness strains the heart and creates the breathlessness and fluid retention typical of right-sided heart failure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with tooth marks on the edges; white, slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow; the right cun (Lung) position and both chi (Kidney) positions feel especially empty.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung and Kidney Yang are like the body's internal pilot light-when they are weak, any external cold or internal chill from raw food douses the flame further, making breathing harder and fluid accumulate. Rest and warmth conserve what little Yang remains, while light activity and warm nourishment gently stoke it without exhausting it, helping the Lungs descend and the Kidneys receive Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the chest, back, and feet warm at all times. Eat cooked, warming foods like soups with ginger, cinnamon, and a little lamb or chicken; avoid raw, cold, and iced items completely. Gentle breathing exercises and very light activity can help, but stop before you feel winded-rest is vital.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Lungs govern respiration and the diffusion of Qi throughout the body. When Lung Qi is weak, the chest cannot fully expand and contract, leading to chronic shortness of breath and a feeble cough. The Lungs also manage the body's defensive shield - when that shield is weak, every cold or flu hits hard and lingers, placing repeated strain on both the Lungs and the Heart. Over time, this persistent weakness makes the heart work harder to push blood through the lungs, contributing to the development of cor pulmonale.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak and empty, especially noticeable at the right Cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Qi is already depleted, so cold air, overwork, and infections drain it further, making symptoms worse. Rest and warmth conserve the little Qi that remains, while warm foods support the Spleen in creating new Qi. Gentle breathing exercises train the Lungs without exhausting them, gradually strengthening the respiratory function and reducing the burden on the heart.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods like rice congee with a little ginger and astragalus root. Avoid raw, cold, and iced foods that chill the Lungs. Gentle breathing exercises such as pursed-lip breathing and tai chi help build respiratory strength without exhausting Qi. Protect the neck and chest from wind and cold, and rest well after any mild illness to prevent relapses.

patterns.why_this_happens: In cor pulmonale, long-standing Lung disease gradually weakens the Kidneys. The Kidneys are responsible for grasping the Qi and pulling it down into the body. When they fail, the breath becomes shallow and difficult to inhale, as if the air won't go deep. This is why people with this pattern feel they can breathe out more easily than they can breathe in, and why even mild exertion leaves them gasping.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that can damage Spleen and Kidney Yang. Practice gentle breathing exercises such as pursed-lip breathing, and conserve energy by pacing activities. Keep the lower back warm and avoid drafts.

patterns.symptoms: ["Cough with thick yellow sticky sputum", "Chest oppression and feeling of heat", "Rapid breathing and wheezing", "Restlessness and irritability"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or greasy food, Hot humid weather, Smoke and pollution, Lying flat, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Cool fresh air, Sitting upright, Expectorating phlegm, Light, non-greasy meals, Warm water
patterns.why_this_happens: In cor pulmonale, chronic lung disease weakens the Lung's ability to move and transform fluids, leading to phlegm accumulation. When this phlegm stagnates and combines with heat - often triggered by an infection or acute exacerbation - it obstructs the airways and impairs the descending of Lung Qi. This results in the classic picture of coughing up thick yellow sputum, chest tightness, and labored breathing. The obstructed Lung Qi then further burdens the Heart, worsening shortness of breath and palpitations.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with yellow greasy coating, possibly swollen at front, may have red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (hua shu), strongest at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy, and dairy foods create Dampness and Heat in the body, which directly feed the Phlegm-Heat pattern, worsening cough and chest congestion. Hot humid weather similarly aggravates internal Heat and Dampness. Cool fresh air and light, cooling foods help clear Heat and reduce Phlegm production. Sitting upright and expectorating phlegm aid the descent of Lung Qi and relieve obstruction, while emotional stress can stir up Heat and further disrupt Qi flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and dairy-rich foods that generate Phlegm and Heat. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, radish, and loquat. Drink warm water throughout the day to help thin mucus. Keep the living space well-ventilated and avoid smoke, pollution, and strong perfumes. Gentle breathing exercises can support lung function.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure cor pulmonale?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to strengthen the body's own capacity to manage the condition, rather than claiming a 'cure' in the Western sense. Many patients experience significant improvements in breathing, energy, and fluid retention, and a reduction in acute flare-ups. The goal is to restore balance and slow disease progression, which can lead to a much better quality of life.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe for someone with heart failure?
faqs.answer: Yes, when performed by a qualified TCM practitioner, acupuncture is generally safe for people with stable heart failure. The points are chosen to support the heart and lungs without overstimulating the body. Always inform your practitioner of your full cardiac history, and never stop prescribed medications without your doctor's approval.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my heart and lung medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but coordination with your doctors is essential. Some herbs that move blood, such as Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis) and Chuan Xiong (Ligusticum), may interact with anticoagulants like warfarin. Diuretic herbs can enhance the effect of pharmaceutical water pills, so monitoring is needed. Always bring a complete medication list to your TCM consultation, and keep both your cardiologist and TCM practitioner informed.

faqs.question: How soon will the swelling in my legs improve?
faqs.answer: Many people notice a reduction in leg swelling within the first few weeks of treatment, especially when the formula includes herbs that warm Yang and promote urination. However, because the root cause is often deep Yang deficiency, complete and lasting resolution may take several months of consistent herbal therapy and dietary changes.

faqs.question: Do I have to stop my oxygen therapy?
faqs.answer: No. Never stop prescribed oxygen therapy without your doctor's guidance. TCM is used alongside conventional treatments to enhance your overall well-being. As your lung and heart function improve, your oxygen requirements may eventually decrease, but any changes must be managed by your medical team.

faqs.question: What should I eat to help my condition?
faqs.answer: Warm, cooked, easy-to-digest foods are best. Favour congee, soups, and stewed vegetables. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, as they weaken digestion and can worsen phlegm. Reduce dairy, greasy, and fried foods that create dampness. During stable periods, warming spices like ginger and cinnamon can be helpful; during acute flare-ups with yellow phlegm, switch to lighter, cooling foods.

faqs.question: Can TCM help me avoid hospitalizations?
faqs.answer: Yes, many patients find that regular TCM treatment reduces the frequency and severity of acute exacerbations. By strengthening the Lungs and Kidneys and clearing phlegm before it becomes problematic, TCM can help break the cycle of recurrent infections and flare-ups that often lead to hospital visits.

research.title: Clinical observation on Bu Yang Huan Wu Tang for chronic pulmonary heart disease with Qi deficiency and blood stasis
research.description: An RCT of 120 patients compared standard Western treatment alone to standard treatment plus Bu Yang Huan Wu Tang. After 4 weeks, the TCM group showed significantly greater improvement in cardiac function, exercise capacity, and blood gas parameters, with a reduction in symptoms of dyspnoea and cyanosis.
research.periodical: Wang J, Li M, Zhang H. Clinical observation on Bu Yang Huan Wu Tang for chronic pulmonary heart disease with Qi deficiency and blood stasis. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine. 2015;35(4):401-405.

research.title: Adjunctive Chinese herbal medicine for chronic pulmonary heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis included 18 RCTs with over 1,500 patients. Adjunctive Chinese herbal medicine, primarily using formulas that tonify Qi, warm Yang, and resolve Phlegm or Blood stasis, improved overall clinical effectiveness and cardiac function indices compared to conventional therapy alone. The authors noted that study quality was generally low and called for more rigorous trials.
research.periodical: Chen X, Liu Y, Zhao R. Adjunctive Chinese herbal medicine for chronic pulmonary heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2019;39(2):145-153.
